name: Teotihuacan

interval.label: c. 100 BCE–800 CE
interval.note: Broad city chronology in Barnes’s essay; buildings and population changed within it.

question: What can a city plan reveal about collective life?
summary: Teotihuacan was made through public construction and the work of households. At Tlajinga, blade production, courtyards and drains connect modest residences to a larger urban system. Nearby platform buildings had different materials and activities. These remains explain practical organization and change while leaving the identities and exact powers of many decision makers uncertain.

sections.title: A city was built at different moments
sections.text: Teotihuacan’s great monuments and apartment compounds belong to different phases of urban life. Barnes places major monumental building around 100–250 CE and apartment development especially around 250–550. Rooms, courtyards and streets therefore need dates as well as positions on a plan. The city’s broad history continues into a period of reduced population after 600. A single drawing cannot make every building contemporary, and a later artifact cannot be fixed to the year 200 merely because it appears beside that view.

citations.locator: Introduction; Residential Architecture

sections.title: A household could also make tools
sections.text: In the southern district of Tlajinga, excavators investigated parts of Compounds 17 and 18. Compound 17 preserves cores and byproducts from making obsidian blades, sharp cutting tools used widely in the city. Producing these useful goods helped residents obtain things they did not make themselves. The project interprets differences in skill as evidence of apprenticeship and work across generations. That gives production a household setting, although it does not identify an individual apprentice, their age, or the rules by which work was assigned.

sections.title: Shared spaces linked homes to the street
sections.text: Building materials varied: some walls used cut stone, others smaller stones, rubble or adobe. Courtyards provided space for gatherings and domestic ritual, while drains from Compounds 17 and 18 emptied toward the Street of the Dead. These connections made household life part of the city’s physical organization. Modest construction did not mean isolation: residents also obtained some greenstone, shell, mica and decorated pottery. Different kinds of access and material work could coexist within the same district.

citations.locator: Construction materials; courtyards, drains and imported goods

sections.title: A neighborhood center had a changing role
sections.text: Across the street, elevated platform buildings used more elaborate surfaces and decoration. Recent research compares their floors, tools and pottery with nearby apartments. Greater domestic residues and grinding-tool densities in the apartments support different food-related activities. At Complex 2, earlier structures were covered with fill before raised buildings were constructed. Excavators interpret its later use as more civic-ceremonial, within the areas investigated. Such changes reveal organization at the neighborhood scale without supplying the names of its decision makers or proving that every household had equal power.

citations.locator: Complexes 2 and 4; Comparing the Neighborhood Center and Apartments

sections.title: The mask answers another kind of question
sections.text: The selected greenstone face has its own third–seventh-century date. Its recessed eyes and mouth may once have held inlays. Weight, absent viewing holes and side perforations lead the museum to suggest attachment to another object rather than wearing by a living person. Possible figures, bundles and religious meanings remain interpretations. The mask makes skilled shaping visible; it does not identify a ruler or connect this particular object to a household excavated at Tlajinga.

deeperReading.title: Move carefully between the scale of a home and a city
deeperReading.text: A compound can show how shared space, materials and productive work were arranged, but an excavated sample is not the city in miniature. Barnes notes that only a small fraction of the suspected apartment compounds have been investigated. Tlajinga supplies particular evidence of modest construction and craft alongside access to imported goods. The project’s placement of its residents within a socioeconomic spectrum is an interpretation of that evidence, not a list of everyone’s wealth, origin or legal status. These observations allow social variation to enter the account without treating a shared architectural form as proof of identical lives.

deeperReading.title: Test a function with evidence that could disagree
deeperReading.text: Tlajinga’s platform buildings invite several explanations: temples, civic spaces, elite residences or combinations of these. The recent study compares architecture with floor chemistry and artifacts. Its pottery-form differences are not statistically significant; those pots alone cannot establish the proposed contrast in activities. Grinding tools and the distribution of food-related residues carry other parts of the argument. Building elaboration and buried earlier structures add a sequence. Combining such evidence makes the interpretation testable while leaving mixed functions and unexcavated areas open.

deeperReading.title: A map and an object keep different kinds of time
deeperReading.text: The inspected 2026 city-and-district map combines the earlier Teotihuacan Mapping Project with later fieldwork. Its spatial relationships are useful, but the composite is not a photograph of one ancient year or a single-phase household plan. The selected mask has a separate catalogue range and no secure excavated findspot in the consulted record. Reading the two together therefore compares kinds of evidence; it cannot place the mask in a named apartment or convert urban coordination into a recovered royal biography.

evidenceReading.title: How do remains become an explanation of work?
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases of modern archaeological and museum accounts, not ancient quotations. Each interpretation depends on the scale and context of the evidence.

items.label: A workshop tested below the surface
items.text: The 2019 abstract reports that subsurface excavation confirmed obsidian production at Compound 17, after earlier workshop identifications from surface debris had been questioned.
items.interpretation: Excavation tests whether a concentration belongs to production in that location. One confirmed compound does not establish that every surface concentration is a workshop. Only this abstract was consulted, not the article’s complete technical analysis.

items.label: Different indicators of food-related activity
items.text: The recent study compares food-related floor residues and tools in apartments and platform buildings; its pottery-form differences alone are not statistically significant.
items.interpretation: The proposed difference in activities depends on several kinds of evidence. A more decorated building is not automatically a temple, and chemical residues do not recover an exact meal. Function remains qualified for the areas and phases investigated.

items.label: A carved face and a proposed attachment
items.text: The photograph shows facial depressions and a side perforation. The catalogue adds weight, dimensions and the absence of viewing holes to its argument that the mask probably was not worn by living people.
items.interpretation: Visible recesses should not be mistaken for demonstrated through-holes. Attachment to a figure or bundle is a proposal, not a recovered original mounting. The object does not identify a ruler, its exact place of use or a Tlajinga household.

familyActivity.title: Draw a relationship; keep a question open
steps: Read the supplied paragraph about shared spaces, with an adult if useful. Draw symbols for nearby rooms, a shared courtyard and a drain leading toward the street. Label this a modern relationship sketch, not a measured ancient plan.
Choose one shared feature. Explain why its use or maintenance might involve more than one household. Mark that explanation as an inference rather than a recovered rule.

Add a separate work note from the blade-making account: cores and byproducts support production at Compound 17. Finish with one question about who decided or performed the work that the supplied evidence cannot answer.
familyActivity.explanation: The supplied text supports the spatial relationships and work example. The sketch does not invent exact rooms, task locations, household numbers or decision makers.

review.reviewer: Codex source consultation and author self-review; not independent historian approval
review.scope: Selected neighborhood-based account of household craft, shared space, sampled platform functions and separate mask interpretation; distinct c.100 BCE–650 CE teaching reference, deeper reading, three evidence readings and a text-supported family sketch. Existing case interval, objects, claims and comparison dimensions remain intact. An original relationship guide and the separately licensed composite source map accompany the account; no measured household reconstruction is supplied.
limitations: The full c.100 BCE–800 CE case survives. The reference’s 650 teaching edge is not a collapse or abandonment date. Broad city chronology, local phases, individual radiocarbon samples, composite mapping and the mask’s third–seventh-century range are not reconciled into one event.

Two short undated PATT pages and selected 2026 report passages were consulted, not the complete residential literature, linked tDAR reports, original chemistry/isotope tables, household census or a citywide labor history. Statements about ongoing work on undated pages are not current 2026 analysis reports.

The 2019 workshop article is used at abstract level only; full-text access failed. Subsurface confirmation in one compound is not validation of all surface workshops or evidence for production rates. Apprenticeship, social status and civic-ceremonial function remain qualified archaeological interpretations.

The existing mask image and official details/rights were checked; its provenance tab was not freshly exposed. Precise findspot, original attachment, named owner, ruler, household membership and specific deity remain unresolved. Original image bytes and object IDs are preserved.

The inspected Figure 1 is composite mapping, with CC BY-NC 4.0 rights and earlier mapping attribution. Its generated Long Description contains incorrect legend labels; actual pixels and caption take precedence. The supplied figure is converted losslessly, without cropping, enhancement or tracing. Small labels retain a readable text equivalent. No single-phase household plan or new numeric neighborhood locator is claimed.

Shared architecture and coordinated work establish neither a homogeneous population nor equal power, one recovered constitution, voluntary labor or a known list of rulers. No contact or causal sequence with Chavín or Moche is inferred. Wider gender, coercion, migration and resident perspectives remain open research.
Independent archaeological/source review, real adult/family use, screen-reader and physical-device behavior, physical print and human acceptance remain open.

placeStudy.title: Teotihuacan: a city reference and a southern neighborhood
placeStudy.description: The point orients the archaeological city. The Tlajinga project places the investigated district in the southern city; no verified numeric location for Compounds 17 and 18 is added here. Use the separately identified source map for their relative setting. The modern guide explains relationships and is not a measured household plan. The mask has no precise excavated findspot in the consulted catalogue.
